title: The item that came back
teaches: Versions and vector clocks, merging conflicting writes, CRDTs and collaborative editing, consistency models, and CAP and PACELC
summary: **Concurrent writes need a merge rule.** A store that accepts writes on two replicas at once will hold two versions of a key, and its engineers must specify how to reconcile them.
**Last writer wins loses writes.** It keeps the version with the later timestamp, silently discards the other, and relies on physical clocks that can drift.

**Vector clocks tell newer from concurrent.** Each version carries one counter per replica, compared entry by entry: if every entry is at least as large and one is larger, the version is newer, and if each clock has a larger entry somewhere, they are concurrent.
**A merge must keep removes as well as adds.** Dynamo's cart merged by union, so a deleted item could reappear; an observed-remove set tracks both additions and removals.

**CRDTs merge without coordination.** Replicated data structures for counters, sets, maps and text guarantee that replicas converge to the same state regardless of message order, at the cost of extra metadata.

**Shared editing requires position transformation or immutable IDs.** Operational transformation rewrites each edit's index against concurrent edits, whereas a text CRDT assigns every character a fixed identifier.

**Name the consistency you offer.** Linearizable, causal, read-your-writes and eventual consistency provide different guarantees, and engineers select the weakest model that preserves correctness for a given feature.

**CAP applies during partitions.** While replicas cannot reach each other, an isolated replica must either reject requests or answer without consulting the others; PACELC adds that during normal operation the trade-off is between latency and consistency.

blocks.text: The Dynamo paper from lesson 12, presented at SOSP in October 2007, contains a sentence most papers would have left out. When two versions of a customer's cart conflict, the cart service merges them, and "using this reconciliation mechanism, an 'add to cart' operation is never lost. However, deleted items can resurface." A customer removes a book, the book comes back, and Amazon's engineers decided that was better than refusing the customer's next click.

The book comes back because of how the Dynamo design accepts writes. During a network partition, or simply when two writes arrive at two coordinators at the same moment, two replicas of one key each accept a different change. When they next communicate, each holds a version the other has not seen. Any data store that accepts writes on more than one replica at a time faces this conflict. Its builders must decide how to tell whether one version superseded the other, and what to retain if neither did.

In the interactive figure below, the cart initially holds a book. The customer's phone adds a kettle through replica X while the customer's laptop, at almost the same moment, removes the book through replica Y, while X and Y cannot reach each other. Then the partition heals. Four rules for merging the two versions produce four different carts.

blocks.caption: One cart, two replicas, a partition. The phone [[adds a kettle|write]] through X and the laptop removes the book through Y; when the partition heals, each replica sends its version to the other and merges by the rule chosen under "Merge by": last writer wins (each replica stamps its write with its own clock), keep both (vector clocks), union, or add and remove sets. Messages move in slow motion.
blocks.task: Try each rule, and find the one that gives the cart the customer meant.

blocks.text: The simplest rule stamps each write with the time on the replica's clock and, when two versions meet, keeps the one with the later stamp. It needs no extra metadata and always gives one answer, which is why Cassandra uses it for every column. In the figure, Y's remove was stamped 30 ms after X's add, so Y's whole cart wins and the kettle disappears. Nothing reports the loss.

This approach has two flaws. First, the rule silently discards one of two concurrent writes every time, so it is appropriate only where a later write truly replaces the earlier one in full, such as a user updating a profile picture. Second, timestamps come from physical clocks on different machines. Clocks synchronised by NTP (the Network Time Protocol, which adjusts a machine's clock against network time servers) typically drift by a few milliseconds and can diverge much further after a hardware fault or a leap second. As a result, the write that occurred second in real time can carry an earlier timestamp and be overwritten. In lesson 20, we will examine what is required to build a clock with bounded error.

In July 1978 Leslie Lamport published "Time, Clocks, and the Ordering of Events in a Distributed System" in Communications of the ACM.[^lamport] Its starting point was that machines have no shared clock to agree on, so the order that matters is causal: event a **happened before** event b if a could have influenced b, because they were on one machine in that order or because a message carried news of a to b's machine. Two events where neither happened before the other are **concurrent**, whatever the clocks said.

In 1988, Colin Fidge and Friedemann Mattern independently published a data structure that captures causal history: the **vector clock**. Every version of a value carries one integer counter for each replica that has modified it. When a replica accepts a write, it increments its own counter; when a replica merges two versions, it takes the element-wise maximum of their counters. We will write a vector clock as each replica's identifier followed by its counter, so [X1 Y1] means replica X has recorded 1 write to this key and replica Y has recorded 1 write; an omitted replica has a counter of 0. Replicas compare two versions entry by entry:

blocks.title: Comparing two vector clocks
points: Every entry of a is at most the matching entry of b, and one is smaller: a happened before b, and b replaces it. [X1] is before [X2].

If each clock has at least one entry strictly larger than the other's, the versions are concurrent. Comparing [X2] against [X1 Y1] shows concurrency because X recorded a second write that Y never saw, while Y recorded a write that X never saw.
If all entries are equal, the two versions are identical.

blocks.text: Dynamo attaches a vector clock to every version. If one version's clock happened before another's, the store drops the older version. If multiple versions are concurrent, the store retains all of them as **siblings** and returns them together on a read. In Dynamo's API, a read returns the list of sibling values along with an opaque **context** containing their vector clocks. The client application merges the values and passes the context back in its subsequent write, allowing the store to assign a new vector clock that supersedes all the merged siblings. Select "Keep both" in the figure to see both versions returned to the phone. No data is lost, but every client reading a cart must implement reconciliation logic.[^truncation]

Amazon's cart service reconciled siblings by taking the set **union** of the items in every version. Taking the union retains the kettle and restores the deleted book, because a version missing the book carries no record of whether the book was never added or was explicitly removed. To distinguish the two, an **observed-remove set** (OR-Set) tracks causal history per element: each addition attaches a globally unique tag to the item, and a removal records the specific tags of the additions currently present on that replica. When two replicas merge their sets, they take the union of all additions and the union of all removals; an item remains in the set if and only if it has an addition tag that does not appear in the removal set. In our example, the laptop's removal recorded the book's addition tag, so the book stays out, while no removal recorded the kettle's tag, so the kettle stays in. If the phone had added a second copy of the book during the partition, that addition would carry a fresh tag and survive the merge.

Marc Shapiro, Nuno Preguiça, Carlos Baquero and Marek Zawirski formalised this family of data structures in 2011 as **conflict-free replicated data types** (CRDTs). In a state-based CRDT, the merge function is commutative ($A \sqcup B = B \sqcup A$), associative ($(A \sqcup B) \sqcup C = A \sqcup (B \sqcup C)$) and idempotent ($A \sqcup A = A$). Because of these three properties, any two replicas that have received the same set of updates converge to the exact same state, regardless of the order in which updates arrive or whether messages are duplicated. A straightforward example is a grow-only counter for social-media likes: in a cluster of $n$ replicas, the counter is an $n$-element vector where each replica increments only its own slot, the displayed total is the sum of all slots, and merging two counters takes the maximum of each slot.

CRDTs trade extra metadata for restricted semantics. An observed-remove set allocates a unique tag for every addition and retains removal records until every replica is guaranteed to have processed them.[^tombstones] Furthermore, while counters, sets, registers, maps and plain text have CRDT formulations, invariants like "a bank account balance must not drop below 0 USD" cannot be enforced by a CRDT alone, because two partitioned replicas can each approve a withdrawal that satisfies the invariant locally but violates it when combined. Depending on the data's invariants, engineers choose from four approaches:

blocks.title: Choosing a merge rule
points: Last writer wins, when a later write completely supersedes an earlier one, such as updating a profile picture or a configuration setting.
A CRDT, when the data structure is a counter, set, map or text document with a mathematically sound automatic merge.
Sibling versions returned to the client application, when domain-specific reconciliation logic is required and writes must not be dropped.
A single-leader consensus group (lesson 11), when concurrent updates must be serialised to preserve a global invariant, such as an account balance that must remain at or above 0 USD.

blocks.text: Collaborative text editors encounter conflict resolution over character indices. For responsiveness, each user's client applies local keystrokes immediately to the local buffer and transmits the operations to peers asynchronously, so concurrent edits arrive at different clients in different orders. Character indices are 0-based: in the string "cart", 'c' is at index 0 and 't' is at index 3. An operation specified by index, such as `delete(3)`, targets the wrong character if a concurrent insertion at an earlier index has already shifted the string.

blocks.caption: Alice and Bob both start from "cart". Alice inserts h after the c, Bob deletes the t, and each then receives the other's edit. Pick how edits are sent and applied. Messages move in slow motion.
blocks.task: Apply the edits as sent and watch the two screens disagree, then find a way that makes them agree.

blocks.text: Clarence Ellis and Simon Gibbs published the first solution in 1989 for GROVE, a collaborative outliner built at the Microelectronics and Computer Technology Corporation (MCC) in Austin: **operational transformation** (OT). Before a client applies a remote operation, it transforms the operation's parameters against all concurrent operations that have already been applied locally. Because Alice's insertion at index 1 precedes index 3, her client transforms Bob's incoming `delete(3)` into `delete(4)`. Designing transformation functions that converge across every pair of operation types and arrival orders in a peer-to-peer network proved difficult, and several published OT algorithms were later shown to fail under multi-way concurrency. In 1995, David Nichols and colleagues at Xerox PARC simplified the state space in their Jupiter system by routing every edit through a single central server that establishes a total order; each client then only transforms its unacknowledged local edits against the server's stream. Google Wave in 2009 and the 2010 rewrite of Google Docs adopted this client-server OT architecture.[^wave]

A **text CRDT** avoids positions altogether. Every letter gets an id when it is typed, made of the editor's id and a counter, and never changes. An insert says which letter it follows and a delete says which letter it removes, so edits mean the same thing in any order, and concurrent inserts at one spot are put in id order, the same on every screen. The price is an id for every letter ever typed, deleted ones included. Libraries such as Automerge and Yjs made this practical for documents of ordinary size.

In October 2019, co-founder Evan Wallace documented how Figma's multiplayer design tool avoids full text or tree CRDTs. Like Jupiter, Figma routes updates through a central server, and represents each design file as a scene graph of objects with key-value properties. Concurrent edits to different properties of the same object commute naturally; concurrent edits to the exact same property of the same object are resolved by **last writer wins**, ordered by arrival time at the central server. Although the server overwrites the earlier of two concurrent property changes, the user whose edit was overwritten sees the winning value render within tens of milliseconds. Wallace described Figma's architecture as CRDT-inspired, noting that relying on a central server to sequence updates avoided the metadata overhead of peer-to-peer CRDTs.
Every store in the last few lessons promised something about what a read returns, and the promises have names. From strongest to weakest:

blocks.title: Consistency models, strongest first
points: **Linearizability**: every operation appears to take effect atomically at a single point in real time between its invocation and its completion. All clients observe a single total order of operations that respects real-time ordering. Consensus systems like Chubby and Raft (lesson 11) provide linearizable reads and writes.

**Causal consistency**: operations that are causally related (where one happened before the other) are observed in the same order by every client, while concurrent operations may be observed in different orders by different clients.
**Read your writes**: a client always sees its own earlier writes, whatever it sees of others' (lesson 4).
**Eventual**: if writes stop, all replicas reach the same value in time. Werner Vogels made the term widely known in 2008.

blocks.caption: Eight features of a social site and a shop, each needing a level of consistency. Engineers choose the weakest model that preserves correctness, because stronger consistency increases request latency or reduces availability.

options.ask: Which is the weakest model this feature can live with?

items.name: Selling the last seat on a flight
items.why: Two buyers on two replicas must not both see the seat free; one order of operations is the only way to be sure.

items.name: A lock that one worker at a time may hold
items.why: Lesson 11: if two workers each read "free", both hold the lock.

items.name: A reply in a chat thread
items.why: A reply shown before the message it answers makes no sense; unrelated messages may arrive in any order.

items.name: Hiding an album from your manager, then posting a photo to it
items.why: The photo was posted after the change and because of it, so no reader may see the photo with the old access list.

items.name: Seeing your own new profile picture after changing it
items.why: You notice if your own change seems lost; others seeing it a few seconds late is harmless.

items.name: A comment you just posted, on your own screen
items.why: The writer must see it at once; other readers can wait for replication.

items.name: The number of likes on a post
items.why: A count a few likes behind for a few seconds harms nobody, and a CRDT counter merges it exactly.

items.name: The view count on a video
items.why: Approximate and late is fine, and counting must never slow down watching.

blocks.text: In July 2000 Eric Brewer gave the keynote at the Principles of Distributed Computing conference in Portland, Oregon, and put forward a conjecture: a shared-data system can have at most two of consistency, availability and tolerance of network partitions. Seth Gilbert and Nancy Lynch proved a precise version in 2002.[^cap] The usual summary, "pick two", misleads, because partitions are not optional: links fail. The theorem says what happens while one lasts. A replica that cannot reach the others must either refuse the request, giving up availability, or answer from what it has, giving up linearizability. Chubby refuses on the minority side; Dynamo answers and merges later.

Daniel Abadi pointed out in 2010, and in IEEE Computer in 2012, that the more frequent trade happens when nothing is broken. Waiting for other replicas before answering costs a round trip, often across data centres, on every request. His **PACELC**: if there is a Partition, choose Availability or Consistency; Else, choose Latency or Consistency. Dynamo and Cassandra are PA/EL: they answer during a partition and answer fast otherwise. Chubby and Raft are PC/EC: they refuse on the minority side and always wait for a majority.

When specifying storage for an application feature, an engineer must choose the required consistency model, the failure behaviour during a partition, and the acceptable request latency during normal operation. A post's like counter can run on a PA/EL store backed by a CRDT counter without users noticing temporary divergence. Booking the final seat on a commercial flight requires a PC/EC store to prevent double-booking, at the cost of higher write latency and occasional unavailability during network faults.

blocks.caption: Seven questions on conflicts and consistency
blocks.task: Choose the best answer to each

items.ask: One version of a key has the vector clock [A2 B1] and another has [A1 B2]. What should the store do?
choices: Keep [A2 B1], because A's counter is the larger one and A is listed first
Keep both: neither clock is at least as large in every entry, so they are concurrent
Keep [A1 B2], because its last entry is the larger one and the last entry is the newest
items.why: Each clock is larger in one entry, so each version holds a write the other never saw.

items.ask: One version has the clock [A2 B1] and another has [A3 B1]. What should the store do?
choices: Keep [A3 B1] and drop [A2 B1], which it supersedes
Keep both and return both on the next read, since they differ
Keep [A2 B1], because the older version is the one more replicas hold
items.why: No entry of [A3 B1] is smaller and one is larger, so [A2 B1] happened before it.

items.ask: Why can last writer wins lose a customer's update without any error?
choices: It keeps every version but returns only the newest one, hiding the others until a repair runs
It refuses writes during a partition, so one of the two updates never reaches the store
It drops one of two concurrent writes, chosen by clocks that can be wrong
items.why: The dropped version is gone; if the clocks disagree, even the write that truly came second can lose.

items.ask: Dynamo's cart merged conflicting versions by taking the union of their items. What went wrong?
choices: An added item could be lost
A removed item could reappear when the versions met
Two copies of the same item were kept, so the quantities in the cart doubled after each merge
items.why: A union keeps everything in either version; only a record of the remove, as in an observed-remove set, keeps the item out.

items.ask: Which is a correct reading of the CAP theorem?
choices: A system must choose any two of consistency, availability and partition tolerance when it is designed
A system that is consistent can never also have low latency, even when there are no failures at all
During a partition, a cut-off replica must refuse requests or risk answering with stale data
items.why: Partitions happen whatever the design; the choice is what a cut-off replica does. The latency trade-off without partitions is PACELC's addition.

items.ask: Two editors type into one line at the same time, with no central server. What lets a text CRDT agree on the result?
choices: Every letter has a fixed id, and edits name letters by id instead of by position
A central server puts every edit in one order before anyone applies it
Each edit carries the time it was typed, and the later edit is applied last
items.why: An edit that names a letter means the same thing whatever was inserted before it; a central order is how Jupiter-style transformation works.

items.ask: Which feature needs causal consistency, but nothing stronger?
choices: The last seat on a flight
A reply in a chat thread, shown to everyone in it
The number of likes on a post, which may lag by a few likes for a few seconds
items.why: A reply shown before the message it answers makes no sense, so cause must come before effect; unrelated messages may still arrive in any order. The seat needs linearizability and the like count needs only eventual consistency.

lamport.title: From relativity
lamport.text: Lamport noted that the idea came from special relativity, where there is no universal time for events in different locations, only a partial order defined by whether a light signal could travel from one event to another. The 1978 paper also introduced scalar logical clocks (single counters that respect the happened-before relation) and used them to construct a distributed mutual-exclusion algorithm.

truncation.title: Clocks that grow
truncation.text: A vector clock gains an entry for every replica that coordinates a write to the key. To bound metadata size, Dynamo truncated vector clocks: when a clock exceeded a threshold of 10 entries, the replica removed the entry with the oldest last-updated timestamp. A truncated clock can cause a descendant version to appear concurrent with its ancestor, triggering an unnecessary merge, though the Dynamo authors reported that they had not encountered this issue in production.

tombstones.title: Cleaning up
tombstones.text: A removal record (tombstone) must remain in the set until every replica has processed the addition it cancels; otherwise, a replica that has not yet seen the removal could re-introduce the added tag during a future merge. Determining that every replica has observed an operation requires cluster-wide coordination, so production systems run garbage collection infrequently as a background process.

cap.title: What the proof means by each word
cap.text: In Gilbert and Lynch's formal model, Consistency specifically means atomic (linearizable) data objects, Availability means every request received by a non-failing node must eventually return a response, and Partition tolerance means the network may drop an arbitrary number of messages between nodes. The theorem does not preclude weaker consistency models during a partition: an available system can still provide read-your-writes or causal consistency to clients pinned to a reachable replica.

wave.title: Google Wave
wave.text: Google Wave, announced in May 2009, allowed multiple users to edit rich-text conversation threads concurrently using Jupiter-style operational transformation. Google cancelled standalone development of Wave in August 2010, and its core engineering approach was integrated into the collaborative editing engine launched for Google Docs later that year.
